results.summary: This design implements an SPI peripheral with eight read/write 8-bit registers and eight read-only 8-bit status registers, derived from the tt07_alu_74181 project. It is tested by connecting an RP2040 SPI master to the SPI pins and using MicroPython code to write and read registers, with the first register also driving a 7-segment display. The design improves on the original by using a single buffer counter and adding high-impedance control for MISO when chip select is high. No external hardware is required beyond the RP2040 and the 7-segment display.

This is an analog design intended to generate colorful stripes when viewed under a microscope. It is tested by viewing the chip under a microscope or smartphone camera. The design has essentially no documentation beyond the one-line description and a single unconnected input pin. It is notable only as a simple optical experiment.

This project implements a basic 8-bit R-2R resistor ladder DAC using 25 identical resistors plus two dummies. It is tested by applying a binary input on ui_in[7:0] and measuring the analog output voltage on ua[0] with a multimeter, ADC, or oscilloscope. Silicon test reports indicate it is working, though the tester noted a discontinuity on the MSB and imperfect grounding. It requires external measurement equipment to observe the output.

This is a remix of Uri's Colorful Stripes experiment, intended to generate a colorful pattern when viewed under a microscope. It is tested by viewing the chip under a microscope or smartphone camera. The documentation is minimal, consisting only of the one-line description and a single unconnected input pin. It is notable only as a variant of an existing optical experiment.

This design displays a bouncing IHP logo on a 640x480 VGA screen with an animated color gradient. It is configured via input pins to tile the logo, use a solid color, or use a white background, and an optional Gamepad Pmod allows pausing and changing direction. It requires a Tiny VGA Pmod and optionally a Gamepad Pmod. The design is notable for its use of the TinyVGA standard and interactive controls.

This project implements an 8-bit linear feedback shift register that produces a pseudo-random sequence. It is used by reading the output pins, which change on each clock cycle, and can be seeded by setting the write enable pin high while providing a seed on the input pins. No external hardware is needed other than a way to read the output pins. The design is a straightforward LFSR implementation with no notable limitations mentioned.

This is a Verilog driver for the Adafruit 2.13-inch e-ink display, which uses the SSD1680 chipset. It generates eight simple patterns in real time and sends them via SPI, with a special mode to copy SRAM contents to the display. It requires the specific e-ink display and a bundle of jumper wires to connect to the PMOD. The design is notable for its low memory overhead and ability to put the display into deep sleep while retaining the image.

This design is an SPI-connected PWM generator with eight outputs, featuring two independent generators and four total PWM channels. The documentation is essentially empty, with no explanation of how it works, how to test it, or what external hardware is needed. The pin names indicate SPI communication and PWM outputs, but no further details are provided. It is not possible to describe the design's operation or testing from the available information.

This project implements a 3-stage Dickson charge pump that boosts voltage. It is tested by applying a 2 MHz clock signal to the clk input and measuring the output voltage on ua[0], which should rise to approximately 3.2 V. No external hardware is specified beyond a clock source and a voltage measurement device. The design is a simple analog voltage booster with minimal documentation.

This design displays a bouncing Zero to ASIC logo on a 640x480 VGA screen with an animated color gradient. It is configured via input pins to tile the logo or use a solid color, and an optional Gamepad Pmod allows pausing and changing direction. It requires a Tiny VGA Pmod and optionally a Gamepad Pmod. The design is notable for its use of the TinyVGA standard and interactive controls.
